title: Sajnos..., de szerencsére...: Narrating a Bad Day

sections.title: Naming the problem, then the relief
sections.content: You already know sajnos ("unfortunately") from Unit 12 — szerencsére ("luckily, fortunately") is its natural opposite, and the two pair perfectly for telling a story about a day that went wrong: name the problem with sajnos, then the relief with szerencsére. Combine them with aztán and utána from the last unit, and a whole bad day fits into three or four short clauses — the same connector toolkit you already have, just put to a new use.

sections.title: A bad day, start to finish
rows: Sajnos elromlott az autóm, ezért elkéstem.
Unfortunately my car broke down, so I was late.
Then I lost my phone too.

items.spanish: Reggel elromlott az autóm, ezért elkéstem a munkából.
items.english: In the morning my car broke down, so I was late for work.

items.spanish: Aztán elveszítettem a telefonomat is, de szerencsére később megtaláltam.
items.english: Then I lost my phone too, but luckily I found it later.

items.spanish: Sajnos eltűnt a kulcsom, de szerencsére megtaláltam.
items.english: Unfortunately my key went missing, but luckily I found it.

sections.content: szerencsére and sajnos both sit at the front of their clause, exactly like the sentence adverbs you already know — they comment on the whole sentence, not just one word in it.
